questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that a correct hardware decision is 'barely better than no decision at all' if it only lives in one engineer's head?
options: Because an undocumented decision can't be reviewed, challenged, handed off, or revisited later as calibration or budget conditions change, while a written brief can
Because engineers are legally required to document every technical decision they make
Because quantum hardware decisions are different from every other kind of engineering decision and uniquely require documentation
Because a written brief guarantees the decision was correct, while an undocumented one does not
questions.explain: The lesson frames the brief as the artifact that lets the decision survive beyond the moment it was made -- reviewable, revisitable, and handoff-able -- which an undocumented decision in someone's head cannot be.

questions.q: What does the lesson say is wrong with a brief that states 'Platform X is best' without further explanation?
options: It fails to name the specific deciding tradeoff (the metric that actually separated the winning platform from the alternatives for this workload), so it hasn't actually explained the decision
It is wrong because platform names should never appear in a hardware-selection brief
It is wrong only because it is too short, regardless of content
It is wrong because every brief must recommend at least two platforms simultaneously
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that the tradeoffs section is what matters most, and that simply naming a winner without the deciding metric fails to explain the decision at all.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a brief with no caveats section is 'less trustworthy, not more confident'?
options: Because every real platform has some limitation or risk, so omitting caveats suggests the analysis was incomplete rather than that the platform is flawless
Because caveats are a formal requirement with no real analytical purpose
Because confidence and trustworthiness are unrelated to whether risks are disclosed
Because caveats are only needed when recommending trapped-ion platforms specifically
questions.explain: The lesson's reasoning is that since every real platform carries tradeoffs, a brief that reports none is more likely incomplete than it is evidence of a flawless choice.

questions.q: In the worked VQE example, what was the actual deciding tradeoff between the superconducting and trapped-ion candidates?
options: Connectivity versus cost: the superconducting platform would need modest, tolerable SWAP overhead for the few non-adjacent qubit pairs, while the trapped-ion platform avoided that overhead but at higher cost and longer queue time
Qubit count, because the trapped-ion platform could not support 8-10 qubits at all
Coherent circuit depth, because the superconducting platform could not sustain a shallow VQE circuit
There was no deciding tradeoff; the two platforms were functionally identical for this workload
questions.explain: The brief explicitly states that at this modest scale, qubit count and coherence were sufficient on both platforms, so the real deciding factor was the connectivity/SWAP-overhead-versus-cost tradeoff.

questions.q: What does the final 'what would change the recommendation' section of a hardware-selection brief accomplish?
options: It states the specific future conditions (e.g., a growing connectivity requirement or a tighter error tolerance) that would flip the recommendation, keeping the brief useful as circumstances change rather than letting it go stale
It restates the requirements summary in different words for emphasis
It is optional filler with no real decision-making function
It lists every platform that was NOT chosen, with no further explanation
questions.explain: The lesson explains this section is what makes the brief durable: naming the conditions that would reverse the recommendation lets the document stay useful instead of becoming a one-time snapshot that goes stale.
